guide.title: Westbrook, Connecticut: Birthplace of the Submarine
guide.intro: Westbrook was first settled about 1648 as the Oyster River Quarter of Old Saybrook, gaining independence in 1724 when a petition set it aside as West Parish with its own church. Before 1810 the community was known as Pochoug, an Indian word the town translates as "at the confluence of two rivers"; it was renamed Westbrook that year and incorporated as its own town in 1840. Timber from local white oak and chestnut forests sustained a shipbuilding industry that flourished for nearly a century. David Bushnell, inventor of the Turtle submarine, was born in 1740 in what is now Westbrook; he launched it in fall 1776, and Ezra Lee piloted it against a British warship in New York Harbor that year. By the 1870s Westbrook was a popular summer resort, a character it still retains, and it hosted Eleanor Roosevelt at Esther Lape's estate, whose 1972 gift created Connecticut's first national wildlife refuge.

sections.heading: The submarine's birthplace
sections.body: David Bushnell enrolled at Yale in 1771 at age 31 and launched the Turtle, his hand-cranked wooden submarine, in the fall of 1776; Ezra Lee piloted it against HMS Eagle in New York Harbor that same year, and Thomas Jefferson's 1798 account helped establish Bushnell as "the Father of Submarine Warfare." The Bushnell House on Boston Post Road, built between 1680 and 1720, stands as a memorial to him — though he never lived there himself, having lived about a mile away on the road to Essex. Esther Everett Lape donated 150 acres in Westbrook in 1972 to establish Salt Meadow National Wildlife Refuge, Connecticut's first; Congress renamed it for Congressman Stewart B. McKinney in 1987, and it now spans ten units over 70 miles of Connecticut coastline. Eleanor Roosevelt was a frequent guest at Lape's estate, the site of which is now the refuge.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Most visitors drive: Westbrook sits on the I-95 shoreline corridor with U.S. Route 1 (Boston Post Road) running through the center of town, and Route 9 also reaches Town Hall. Westbrook is also one of the rare small shoreline towns with its own rail stop — a CTrail Shore Line East station at 101 Norris Avenue, with free daily commuter parking seven days a week and a pedestrian bridge between its two tracks. No Amtrak or Metro-North train stops in Westbrook itself; the nearest Amtrak stop is Old Saybrook, about five miles east, and the nearest Shore Line East stops either side are Clinton and Old Saybrook.

sections.heading: The shoreline town today
sections.body: The town-run beach is open to non-residents by pass — a $40 daily parking pass at the gate or a $150 seasonal pass from the First Selectman's Office, cash or check only; residents enter free with ID. The Westbrook Drum Corps, established in 1910, holds its Ancient fife-and-drum Muster free and open to the public on the fourth weekend of August at Ted Lane Field, drawing 40-plus invited corps.

faq.question: How do I get to Westbrook?
faq.answer: By car via I-95 or Route 1 (Boston Post Road), or by train — Westbrook has its own CTrail Shore Line East station at 101 Norris Avenue, with free daily commuter parking. No Amtrak or Metro-North serve Westbrook directly; the nearest Amtrak stop is Old Saybrook, about five miles east.

faq.question: Who was David Bushnell?
faq.answer: Born in Westbrook (then part of Saybrook) in 1740, Bushnell invented the Turtle, the world's first submarine, launching it in 1776; Ezra Lee piloted it against a British warship in New York Harbor that year. The Bushnell House on Boston Post Road, an antique house museum, stands as a memorial to him.

faq.question: What is the Stewart B. McKinney National Wildlife Refuge?
faq.answer: Connecticut's first national wildlife refuge, created from a 150-acre 1972 gift by Esther Everett Lape in Westbrook. Renamed for Congressman Stewart B. McKinney in 1987, it now spans ten units over 70 miles of coastline, with headquarters and the 1.72-mile Salt Meadow Trail still in Westbrook.

faq.question: Is there a parking pass required at Westbrook's beach?
faq.answer: Yes for non-residents — a $40 daily pass purchased at the gate, or a $150 seasonal pass from the First Selectman's Office (cash or check only). Residents enter free with ID.

faq.question: Is there a hotel in Westbrook?
faq.answer: Yes — the Captain Stannard House and Westbrook Inn are both verified bed-and-breakfasts in 19th-century houses on Boston Post Road. A larger resort, Water's Edge Resort & Spa, is also listed on Long Island Sound, though its current 2026 operating details could not be independently confirmed — call ahead.

places.name: Salt Meadow Unit, Stewart B. McKinney National Wildlife Refuge
places.summary: The original core of the refuge and site of its headquarters: Esther Everett Lape donated 150 acres here in 1972 to create Connecticut's first national wildlife refuge, renamed for Congressman Stewart B. McKinney in 1987. The refuge's longest trail, the 1.72-mile Salt Meadow Trail, is here, along with the Pond Overlook and Crossover trails. Phone (860) 399-2513.

places.name: Bushnell House
places.summary: Built between 1680 and 1720, this house stands as a memorial to submarine inventor David Bushnell, though he never lived in it — he lived about a mile away on the road to Essex. Leighton Lee III, who ran his Museum of Early Engineering Technology in the building, donated it to the Town of Westbrook in 2021; the Westbrook Historical Society opened it as an antique house museum in June 2024.

places.name: Westbrook Historical Society Museum
places.summary: The society's mission is to acquire, preserve and display documents, relics and records relating to the history of Westbrook. Open Wednesdays 9 a.m.–noon or by appointment; phone (860) 399-7473.

places.name: The Westbrook Muster (Westbrook Drum Corps)
places.address: Ted Lane Field, Westbrook, CT (Corps House, 1196 Boston Post Rd, Westbrook, CT 06498)
places.summary: The Westbrook Drum Corps, established in 1910, holds its annual Ancient fife-and-drum Muster on the fourth weekend of August at Ted Lane Field, free and open to the public, drawing 40-plus invited corps from across the U.S. and beyond. Confirm the exact date each year before travelling.

places.name: Westbrook Town Beach
places.summary: The town-run shoreline beach requires a parking pass for non-residents: $40 daily at the gate, or $150 seasonal from the First Selectman's Office at Town Hall, cash or check only, covering two license plates. Residents enter free with ID. Dogs are not permitted May 1–September 30. Confirm the current access point with the Selectman's Office at (860) 399-3040.

places.name: Westbrook Public Library
places.summary: Established in 1895, the library occupied a building on the Town Green from 1905 to 1977 before moving to Goodspeed Drive; it reopened at the renovated Goodspeed facility in September 2008. Phone (860) 399-6422.

places.name: Bill's Seafood
places.summary: Family owned since 1978, on the banks of the Patchogue River beside the landmark Singing Bridge, with outdoor picnic tables, fried clams, lobster rolls and an ice cream window. Cash only (ATM on site), no reservations. Open daily from 11 a.m.; phone (860) 399-7224.

places.name: Cafe Routier
places.summary: A contemporary French bistro and lounge, a long-running shoreline dinner destination. Open weekdays 4:45–9 p.m., weekends 4–9:30 p.m.; reservations required for parties of six or more. Phone (860) 399-8700.

places.name: Bistro Mediterranean Tapas & Bar
places.summary: A Mediterranean small-plates and tapas spot on Boston Post Road — one of three locations, alongside Milford and East Haven. Full menu and online ordering; phone (860) 577-5054.

places.name: Captain Stannard House Bed & Breakfast
places.summary: Built in 1872 as a residence by sea captain Elbert Stannard, welcoming its first guests as an inn in 1902. Ten guest rooms named for shoreline places, with a continental breakfast including home-baked muffins and gluten-free options. Phone (860) 399-4777.

places.name: Westbrook Inn Bed & Breakfast
places.summary: An 1876 house run as a ten-room inn under owner Meri Wick, with sister properties Captain Stannard House and Osprey Cottage. Complimentary gourmet hot breakfast, a riverside dock with kayaks and bikes, gas fireplaces and a monthly "Tuesday Tea." Phone (860) 399-4777.
